summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court vacated a termination order and remanded, holding that the rebuttable presumption in I.C. § 16-1629(9) favors only the Department's filing of a termination petition after fifteen of twenty-two months in care and does not shift to the parent the burden of disproving that termination is in the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: Correctly limits the ASFA-derived fifteen-of-twenty-two-month trigger to the decision whether to file a petition.
key_cases.quote: It does not create a presumption that it is in the best interests of the child to terminate parental rights

key_cases.case_name: Roe v. State, Department of Health & Welfare
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of a grandmother's motion to intervene, holding that the CPA confers no conditional right to intervene, that permissive intervention under I.R.C.P. 24(b)(2) is inconsistent with the CPA, and that once the Department has legal custody it, not the court, decides where the child lives.
key_cases.relevance: Explains the narrow scope of a CPA petition: protection of the child, not adjudication of competing custody claims.
key_cases.quote: Once the Department has legal custody of a child under the CPA, the Department and not the court has the authority to determine where the child should live

key_cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. John Doe (2023-25)
key_cases.holding: Affirming a redisposition order removing five children from a home that had been under protective supervision, the court held for the first time that a redisposition hearing under I.C. § 16-1623 is governed by the same preponderance-of-the-evidence standard as an adjudicatory hearing and does not unconstitutionally interfere with parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: Sets out the disposition options available once a petition is sustained, including protective supervision short of Department custody.
key_cases.quote: The redisposition hearing process is, in essence, another adjudicatory hearing resulting in a "redisposition" of the child's custody

key_cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination as to both parents, the court held that I.C. § 16-1624 authorizes the Department to petition for termination once the court has found CPA jurisdiction at the adjudicatory hearing and placed the child in the Department's legal custody or protective supervision, so neither due process nor the termination statute's purpose provision requires that the parent first be given a full opportunity to complete a case plan.
key_cases.relevance: Identifies I.C. § 16-1624 as the statutory authority for filing a termination petition once CPA jurisdiction is found at the adjudicatory hearing.
key_cases.quote: Thus, under the authority granted by the CPA, the Department is authorized to petition for termination if the court has jurisdiction over the child under the CPA

timeline_requirements.deadline: As soon as possible, but in no event later than thirty (30) days from the date the petition was filed

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Rule states no penalty; the department must still notify every person identified as a caretaker of the disposition as it pertains to them (IDAPA 16.06.01.560)
